W1.title: Scan & join
W1.heading: Scan the air, then join your network
W1.goal: The first Wi-Fi lab, with its own firmware (wifi-lab-w1); the code every lab shares lives in kit/lib/wifi-kit. The ESP32 lists every 2.4 GHz network nearby, then joins yours: you pick it from the scan table and type the password once. It's stored on the chip, never in code. A status view shows the clock (internet time), IP address, bench.local and a live signal chart.
steps: Keep the screen wired as in lesson 03. The push button (pin 5 + GND) is optional: it does exactly what BOOT does.
Flash with the command above (or tell Claude “go”).
Watch the first scan. Click through the views: networks, channels, radar, status.
Open uv run pio device monitor. Find your network's number in the scan table.
Type join 3 (your number), then your password on the next line. It is saved on the chip; the log only shows its length.
The status view opens by itself: clock, IP address, bench.local, signal chart. Try ping bench.local from your Mac, and type ping in the monitor to test the router from the board's side.
Unplug and replug: it rejoins by itself. forget erases the saved network.
W1.note: 5 GHz networks never appear: the S3 radio is 2.4 GHz only. The monitor shows your neighbours' network names and what you type, including the password. Don't paste that part into anything shared.

micropython.label: MicroPython
micropython.goal: Scan the air and join your network from MicroPython's network module. wifi_w1_scan.py lists every network nearby, 2.4 and 5 GHz, then joins yours: you pick it from the scan table and type the password once. It is kept in the chip's NVS, never in the script. A status view shows internet time, the IP address, bench.local and a live signal chart.
micropython.goalLine: Find your network in the scan, join it without writing the password in code, and reach the board by name.
goalCheck: The scan table lists networks with signal, channel, band and security, strongest first.
join plus your password on the next line joins it, and the LED turns green.
status shows the IP, bench.local and the time, and ping bench.local from your computer gets answers.
Run the script again: it rejoins by itself, with no password typed.
steps: Open Code, connect the serial REPL and press Install wifi_kit.py once: every Wi-Fi lab imports it.
Run wifi_w1_scan.py. Checkpoint 1: the first scan table, with a band column. The LED is blue while it scans.
Type channels: how crowded each 2.4 GHz channel is, and which 5 GHz channels are in use.

Find your network's number and type join 3 (your number), then your password on the next line, or both at once: join 3 yourpassword. The number counts in the last table printed. Not in the table? join Your Network. The script never prints the password.

Not joining? Every 3 s the console says how it is going, and after a failure it says why: wrong password? or network not found. Check the name and password, then join again; forget clears a wrong one.
Checkpoint 2: + joined and the status view: IP address, bench.local, channel and band. The LED turns green.
Type tz -6 (your offset from UTC) for local time, and signal for the last minute as a chart. From your computer, try ping bench.local; from the board, reach tests the router.

Type stop (or press Stop) and run the script again: it rejoins by itself. forget erases the saved network; so does FORGET_SAVED = True at the top of the script, before it tries to join. BOOT: click = next view, double-click = scan now, long press = auto-scan on/off.
micropython.note: The web terminal lists every line you send, including the password: don't share that screen. The network is saved in the NVS namespace mpwifi, apart from the Arduino labs' one. MicroPython has no ICMP ping, so reach times a TCP connection to port 80: a reply or a refusal both mean the host is there.

W2.title: Phone control
W2.heading: Control the bench from your phone and your Mac

lan.label: Variation 1 · On your Wi-Fi
lan.goal: Its own firmware (wifi-lab-w2): everything from W1, plus a small web server: a REST API, a live WebSocket, a phone page at bench.local and a set-up network for joining Wi-Fi without a cable. A React + Node dashboard in esp-labs/apps/dashboard gives the same controls on your Mac, with live charts and firmware updates.
steps: Same wiring as W1 (push button optional). Flash with the command above (or tell Claude “go”).
Not joined yet? The status view shows the set-up network bench-setup and its password. Join it from your phone, pick your Wi-Fi on the page that opens, type the password.
Joined: open http://bench.local on your phone. Change the view, send a message, pick an LED colour, dim the screen.
In the serial monitor type token and copy the value.
On the Mac: cd esp-labs/apps/dashboard, cp .env.example .env, paste the token as ESP_TOKEN=, then pnpm install and pnpm dev. Open http://localhost:5173.
Press the button or BOOT: the click appears live on the phone page and the dashboard.
Try a wireless update: uv run pio run -d labs/wifi-lab-w2 -e wifi-lab-w2, then upload .pio/build/wifi-lab-w2/firmware.bin in the dashboard's Admin panel. The screen shows the progress.
lan.note: Everyday controls are open to anyone on your home network: it's a bench toy. Reboot, forget Wi-Fi and firmware updates need the token, which lives on the chip and in the dashboard's .env (git-ignored), never in the browser. Page won't open? Type http://; on a FRITZ!Box tick “WLAN devices may communicate with each other”; on the Mac allow the browser under Privacy & Security → Local Network.

remote.label: Variation 2 · From anywhere
remote.short: board dials out to your server
remote.goal: The same board and phone page, plus a remote link: the board dials out to your dashboard server and keeps a secure WebSocket open. The server needs a public https address: today your Mac plus a tunnel (cloudflared or ngrok), later the same app on a hosted server. The board can't tell the difference. Drive the bench from mobile data, the office, anywhere. Nothing opens on your router, and Wi-Fi isolation stops mattering.
steps: Same wiring (push button optional). Flash with the command above (or tell Claude “go”). It downloads one library the first time: links2004/WebSockets 2.7.3.
On the Mac, in esp-labs/apps/dashboard/.env: ESP_MODE=relay, ESP_TOKEN= the serial token, and DASHBOARD_KEY= the output of openssl rand -hex 16.
Start the server: cd esp-labs/apps/dashboard && pnpm remote (builds the app and serves it on port 8787).

In a second terminal, open a tunnel: pnpm tunnel:cloudflare (no account; prints https://…trycloudflare.com, new each time) or pnpm tunnel:ngrok (your ngrok account; add --url=<your free static domain> and the address never changes).
Tell the board in the serial monitor: relay wss://<tunnel host>. It saves the address and connects; relay then says online and a teal ring appears around the link dot on the screen.
On your phone, turn Wi-Fi off (mobile data), open the tunnel address, sign in with the key, and change the view or the LED. You're controlling the bench from outside your home.
Unplug the board and plug it back in: it rejoins Wi-Fi and dials in again by itself. relay off stops the link.
remote.note: Quick-tunnel addresses change every time you restart cloudflared: type the new one with relay, or use ngrok's free static domain once. Firmware updates stay on your Wi-Fi for now (variation 1). Stop the tunnel (Ctrl+C) when you're done and the public address stops working. Hosting the server instead: run the same app there (pnpm build && pnpm start, ESP_MODE=relay, HOST=0.0.0.0, TRUST_PROXY=true) and point relay at its address. Want to test without a tunnel first? Set HOST=0.0.0.0 in .env and type relay ws://<your Mac's IP>:8787.

micropython.label: MicroPython · Pulsar C5
micropython.short: Wi-Fi signal on TFT and LED control from a phone

head: ST7735 TFT
Pulsar C5
Purpose
rows: backlight; leave open if already connected

micropython.goal: wifi_w2_display.py combines a live Wi-Fi signal display on an 80×160 ST7735 TFT with a local phone page for controlling the on-board RGB LED. The screen shows RSSI in dBm, bars, a 24-second trend and the board's IP. wifi_w2_basic.py works without a TFT; wifi_w2_phone.py adds nearby-network scans and remote control.
micropython.goalLine: See live Wi-Fi signal on the TFT while controlling the RGB LED from your phone.
goalCheck: The TFT shows RSSI, bars, a signal history and the board's IP without flicker.
The phone page's colour buttons change the on-board RGB LED and its label on the TFT.
steps: Unplug USB and wire the 80×160 ST7735 as in O2, with CS on D4/GPIO9. Its SDA/SCL labels mean SPI data/clock.
Open Code, select wifi_w2_display.py and connect the serial REPL. Install st7735.py if it is not already on the board.
Enter WIFI_SSID and WIFI_PASSWORD in the script, or connect with W1 first and keep Wi-Fi active.
Run the script. Checkpoint 1: the TFT shows RSSI, bars, a live trend and IP, while the console prints the board's http:// address.
On a phone connected to the same Wi-Fi, open that address and tap Red, Green, Blue or Off. Checkpoint 2: the on-board LED and TFT colour label change.
Press Stop to close the server. Without a TFT, choose wifi_w2_basic.py. For REST, WebSocket and remote relay, choose wifi_w2_phone.py and install wifi_kit.py first.
micropython.note: The phone page is local and has no login. Do not expose port 80 to the internet. The screen uses the green-tab 80×160 ST7735 offsets from O2; adjust xoffset/yoffset for a different module. Keep your Wi-Fi password out of a shared copy of the script.

W3.title: Internet & AI
W3.heading: Weather from the internet, a poet from the cloud
W3.goal: The board becomes an internet client. It fetches the weather for your city over HTTPS as JSON (Open-Meteo, no account or key) and draws it: an animated sky, the next 24 hours, the week. Then the Bench Oracle: the board sends an AI model what it knows about this moment (place, time, weather, its own temperature) and gets back a haiku, or an answer to your question, plus an LED colour and a scene, as structured JSON. The request goes through LiteLLM on your Mac, so any provider and model works and the provider keys never touch the chip.

0.title: Follow one request, step by step

steps: Same wiring (push button optional). Flash with the command above (or tell Claude “go”). It uses the Wi-Fi network W1/W2 saved.
Open uv run pio device monitor and type city Hamburg (your city). The board looks it up, saves it and fetches the weather.
Click through the views: now (animated sky), forecast (next 24 h), week. The footer shows each request: how long it took and how big the answer was.

Start the AI gateway on the Mac: cd esp-labs/apps/ai-gateway, cp .env.example .env (a LITELLM_MASTER_KEY plus your provider key, e.g. ANTHROPIC_API_KEY), uv sync, then uv run --env-file .env litellm --config config.yaml --port 4000.
Tell the board where it is, in the monitor: ai url http://<your Mac's IP>:4000 and ai key <LITELLM_MASTER_KEY>. Type keys there, never in a chat.
Go to the oracle view and double-click: the model writes a haiku about this moment and picks the LED colour. Hold the button from any view for the same.
Ask it things: ask should I bike to work? or ask what should I build next?. It knows your weather and the board's state.
Switch models without reflashing: ai model oracle-fast, or add any provider to config.yaml (OpenAI, Gemini, a local Ollama model) and pick its name. Compare the time and tokens under each answer.
W3.note: Provider keys stay in the gateway's .env on your Mac. The board only stores the gateway's own key (NVS, never printed: the log shows its last 4 characters), and ai key forget erases it. On your Wi-Fi the board talks plain http to the gateway; for anywhere, put the gateway behind https (a tunnel or a server, as in W2 variation 2). Set a spend limit at each provider; the board asks at most once per 10 s and never by itself.

micropython.label: MicroPython
micropython.goal: wifi_w3_basic.py fetches current weather from Open-Meteo over HTTPS and prints the temperature, humidity and wind. Set your coordinates in the script; no account or API key is needed. The optional wifi_w3_oracle.py adds forecasts and an AI oracle.
micropython.goalLine: Print the current weather for your coordinates in the serial console.
goalCheck: The board joins Wi-Fi and prints its IP address.
The console prints current temperature, humidity and wind for the selected coordinates.
steps: Open Code, select wifi_w3_basic.py and connect the serial REPL. This basic script needs no extra library.
Set LATITUDE, LONGITUDE and PLACE for your location.
Enter WIFI_SSID and WIFI_PASSWORD, or connect with W1 first and keep Wi-Fi active.
Run the script. Checkpoint: the console prints temperature, humidity and wind, then the script ends.
For forecasts and the AI oracle, select the optional wifi_w3_oracle.py; install wifi_kit.py and save a network with W1 first.
micropython.note: The basic script makes one weather request each time you run it. MicroPython's HTTPS support may not validate the server certificate on every firmware build. Keep your Wi-Fi password out of a shared copy of the script.

I1.title: Wi-Fi to the cloud
I1.heading: Publish readings to ThingSpeak
I1.goal: Join your Wi-Fi network, 2.4 GHz or 5 GHz, and post temperature and humidity from a DHT11 to a ThingSpeak channel every 20 seconds.
steps: Create a free ThingSpeak channel with two fields and copy its Write API Key.
Install DHT sensor library from the Library Manager.
Put your network name, password and key into the three constants at the top of the sketch.
Unplug USB, wire the DHT11, plug in and run the command.
The monitor prints the IP, channel and band, then HTTP 200 every 20 seconds. Watch the channel's charts fill.
I1.note: Unlike the C6, the C5 also joins 5 GHz networks: channel 36 and up. Never commit a sketch with your real password or key.

micropython.label: MicroPython
micropython.goal: Join your Wi-Fi network, 2.4 GHz or 5 GHz, from MicroPython and post the DHT11's temperature and humidity to ThingSpeak every 20 seconds.
steps: Create a free ThingSpeak channel with two fields and copy its Write API Key.
Unplug USB, wire the DHT11 and plug in again. Open Code and connect the serial REPL.
In thingspeak_dht.py, put your network name, password and key into the three constants at the top.
Press Run on board. The terminal prints the IP, channel and band, then HTTP 200 every 20 seconds. Press Stop when you are done.
micropython.note: MicroPython's dht and requests modules come with the ESP32-C5 firmware: nothing to install. Never save or share the script with your real password or key.
